card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

W2622849719.title: Phase‐Transformation Ductilization of Brittle High‐Entropy Alloys via Metastability Engineering

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?. System: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V). Processing: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).. Findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.; The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).; Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.; Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.; The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).; The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.; The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).; The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.. Mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.. Future work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.. Quote: "Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases"

W2893800769.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

W2302110147.title: Strain hardening in Fe–16Mn–10Al–0.86C–5Ni high specific strength steel

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. Mechanism: The simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility originates from a characteristic hierarchical microstructure that creates profuse domain boundaries separating domains of different hardness, leading to significant back stress strengthening and delayed necking due to strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%)"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

card: Paper card. Question: Can nanodomained nickel unite nanocrystal strength with coarse-grain ductility?. System: Nickel (Ni) with nanoscale domains. Processing: Pulsed electrodeposition with a grain refiner. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at a strain rate of 5 × 10−4 s−1 at room temperature. Findings: The nanodomained Ni achieves a yield strength approaching 1.3 GPa; The material exhibits a uniform elongation as large as ~30%; The nanoscale domains effectively block dislocations and provide dislocation sources and trapping sites; The nanodomains occupy only ~2.4% of the total volume; The average domain diameter is ~7 nm. Mechanism: The nanoscale domains act as strong obstacles to dislocation movements, and their boundaries provide dislocation sources and trapping sites, leading to enhanced strain hardening. Limitations: The stability of the nanodomains during long-time sample storage and deformation is not fully understood. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of this strategy for other metals and alloys. Quote: "the nanodomains would elevate the strength to GPa level"

W2805419750.title: Tunable stacking fault energies by tailoring local chemical order in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?. System: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.. Test conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).. Findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.; Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).; Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.; Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.; Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.; Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.; Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.. Mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.. Limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.. Future work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.. Quote: "The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities."

Paper card. Question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K). Processing: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations). Test conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing. Findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics; Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]; Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]; Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale; Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization; Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress; Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations. Mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.. Quote: "In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed"

W2936950287.title: Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

card: Paper card. Question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?. System: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. Processing: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K. Findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).; Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).; Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.; Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.; Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.; Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.; The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.. Mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.. Future work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.. Quote: "This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel be enhanced without sacrificing ductility, thereby evading the long-standing strength–ductility trade-off dilemma?. System: FeMnC TWIP steel (23.84% Mn, 0.61% C, balanced Fe) with a low stacking fault energy of 15–30 m Jm−2. Processing: Cylindrical samples were subjected to torsion (180° or 360°) at an angular loading rate of 0.05° s−1 to generate a gradient nanotwinned structure, followed by uniaxial tensile deformation at a strain rate of ~10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Torsion tests at 0.05° s−1; tensile tests at ~10−4 s−1; micro-hardness measured with 500 g load for 15 s; microstructure analyzed via SEM, EBSD, and TEM (200 kV). Findings: Yielding strength of the pre-torsioned TWIP steel was doubled to ~730 MPa (from ~300 MPa) with no reduction in ductility.; A gradient nanotwinned structure formed with twin density increasing from the center to the outermost region (r/R=1).; Twin thickness increased with radial distance, reaching tens of nanometers at the surface.; Subsequent tensile deformation activated secondary and tertiary twins, creating a hierarchical nanotwinned structure.; The hardening modulus remained high until sample failure, unlike traditional processing which reduces ductility.; Finite element simulations showed yielding strength follows a law of mixture, with the hard shell significantly raising the yield strength of the soft core.; Different twinning systems were activated during torsion (e.g., T2, T4) compared to subsequent tension (e.g., T5, T1).; Dislocation dissociation at twin boundaries avoided stress concentration, playing a crucial role in retaining ductility.. Mechanism: The gradient hierarchical nanotwinned structure enhances strength through the hard shell/soft core effect and twin barriers, while ductility is retained because sequential torsion and tension activate different twinning systems, creating a 3D hierarchical network that distributes plasticity and prevents premature failure via localized necking.. Limitations: The method relies on materials prone to deformation twinning (low stacking fault energy); applying the same pre-torsion to 6061 Aluminum alloy resulted in enhanced strength but reduced ductility due to the lack of a hierarchical nanotwin network.. Future work: Develop other methods to produce non-uniform shear strains in metals prone to deformation twinning to enhance material performance, potentially applicable to axially symmetric structural components like axles in machines and high-speed trains.. Quote: "we find that the yielding strength of the material can be doubled at no reduction in ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the rapid solidification inherent to additive manufacturing (specifically SLM and DLF) influence phase selection, microstructure, and mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional processing methods?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) / Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) defined as having at least five principal elements in equimolar/equiatomic compositions (5%–35% concentration each); specifically discussed in the context of bulk HEAs processed by SLM, SEBM, and DLF.. Processing: Additive manufacturing techniques including Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM), and Direct Laser Fabrication (DLF); DLF allows the use of elemental powders fed from different hoppers to produce in situ chemically homogeneous alloys, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed powders.. Test conditions: Not stated in the provided text; the text is a review summarizing published data rather than reporting new experimental test conditions for specific HEA samples.. Findings: HEAs are particularly well suited to AM, with the field expected to grow significantly in the coming years.; Laser-induced rapid solidification in AM can avoid compositional segregation and restrict the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds.; AM of HEAs allows the use of elemental powders as feedstock in DLF, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed metal powders.; Rapid solidification inherent to AM provides a tool to aid phase selection during alloy fabrication.; Traditionally, arc-melting requires extensive re-melting and intermittent ingot inversions, while SPS requires powder alloying and refinement via ball milling.; AM offers advantages over traditional methods by addressing shape and size limitations of HEA components.; The configurational entropy in HEAs stabilizes simple solid solutions (bcc, fcc, hcp), but competition with enthalpy often dictates the final microstructure.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the rapid solidification inherent to the AM process restricts the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds and avoids compositional segregation, while the high configurational entropy stabilizes simple solid solution phases. In DLF specifically, the mechanism involves the controlled supply of elemental powders from different hoppers to produce chemically homogeneous alloys in situ under optimized processing conditions.. Limitations: The text notes that AM of HEAs is a nascent field, stating that 'only two papers on SEBM and SLM' had been published at the time of writing, and that the properties obtained and effects of processing on microstructures are still being discussed.. Future work: The authors state that 'we may expect this field to grow significantly in the coming years' and that the properties and microstructural effects of AM on HEAs are currently being discussed, implying a need for further characterization of these relationships.. Quote: "The impact of rapid solidification inherent to AM on phase selection is highlighted for high-entropy alloys."

Question: How does the use of LENS™ additive manufacturing influence the microstructure, phase constitution, and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys compared to conventional casting, and can it enable the creation of compositionally graded materials?. System: Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi, ZrTiVCrFeNi, TiZrNbMoV, AlCoCrCuFeNiTi, AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.3, 0.6, 0.85), AlxFeCoCrNi(2-x) (x = 0.3, 1), AlxCuCrFeNi2 (0 < x < 1.5), AlCrSiTiV, Al2CoCrCuFeNi. Processing: Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS™) using powder-fed systems with elemental powder blends or pre-alloyed powders; Laser cladding with laser power 0.4–3 kW, beam size 0.6–4.5 mm, scanning velocity 1.7–12 mm/s, and effective energy 46–208 J/mm²; Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) using gas-atomized powder; Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using gas-atomized powder. Test conditions: Compression testing, tensile testing, microhardness testing, magnetic property measurement (saturation magnetization and coercivity), dry sliding wear tests at room temperature and 500°C, hydrogen storage exposure, annealing exposure. Findings: LENS™ processing of Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi resulted in dendritic grains containing an ordered B2 structure and a disordered bcc matrix, avoiding the slow cooling and segregation typical of arc-melting.; ZrTiVCrFeNi and TiZrNbMoV alloys synthesized via LENS™ exhibited dendritic two-phase structures and performed well for hydrogen storage due to non-equilibrium solute-trapping effects.; SLM CoCrFeNi achieved a yield strength of 600 MPa, triple that of its cast equivalent (188 MPa), while maintaining high ductility (32% elongation).; SEBM-processed AlCoCrFeNi showed superior ductility (14%–26% elongation) compared to the as-cast state (5% elongation), attributed to grain refinement and the presence of an fcc phase.; In AlxCuCrFeNi2 graded deposits, microhardness increased progressively with Al content as the microstructure transitioned from fcc/L12 to bcc/B2.; Magnetic properties varied with Al content: low Al regions were weakly ferromagnetic, while high Al bcc/B2 regions were strongly ferromagnetic with high saturation magnetization.; Laser-cladded HEA coatings achieved room temperature hardness values exceeding ceramic particle-reinforced Mg-, Al-, and Ti-matrix alloys and Nb, Ta, and Mo alloys.; AlCrSiTiV clad coatings showed a friction coefficient of ~0.3 and specific wear rate of ~2.10⁻⁵ mm³/Nm, which were 2 and 3 times lower than the Ti-6Al-4V substrate, respectively.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the observed microstructural changes and property enhancements to the rapid cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s) inherent to laser-based additive manufacturing, which cause significant grain refinement, non-equilibrium solute-trapping, and the formation of non-equilibrium phases like bcc that are favored over fcc. The high temperature gradients and solidification rates control the columnar-to-equiaxed transition, while the high viscosity and sluggish diffusion rates of HEA melts limit dilution with substrates.. Limitations: The text notes that the statistical comparison of phases in laser-cladded coatings is biased because 90% of reported coatings contain Al, which stabilizes the bcc phase. Additionally, the presence of metallurgical defects, heterogeneity, and anisotropy in microstructures limits the use of these techniques for fracture applications, and durability properties like corrosion resistance and fracture toughness require further characterization.. Future work: The authors propose that systematic efforts must be made to characterize powder characteristics more finely and incorporate these into simulations. They suggest implementing tools to characterize materials in real-time during processing and using advanced techniques like synchrotron diffraction. Further focus should be devoted to evaluating microstructure and tensile properties to understand the mechanisms of microstructure development, and to exploring in situ thermal treatments to design multiphase steel architectures.. Quote: "The faster cooling rates obtained via direct laser metal deposition lead to a significant non-equilibrium solute-trapping effect, which in turn avoided the component segregation and relieved the solubility limitations."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the phase-specific mechanical behaviors, deformation mechanisms, and phase-boundary interactions in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy under small-scale loading?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (lamellar arrangement of L12 and B2 solid-solution phases). Processing: Vacuum arc-melting of pure elements (>99.9% purity) with homogenization via multiple flips and re-melting cycles; samples polished to 0.02 µm roughness; micro-pillars prepared via FIB (30 kV Ga+ down to 5 kV) with final diameter 2.0 ± 0.3 µm and aspect ratio ~2; bulk specimens prepared via EDM (tensile) and machining (compression). Test conditions: Bulk tensile/compression at 10^-3 s^-1; nano-indentation at 10000 µN and 500 µN loads; strain rate sensitivity at 4×10^-2, 1.2×10^-1, and 4×10^-1 s^-1; micro-pillar compression at ~2.5×10^-4 s^-1; scratch tests at 500 mN load with ramping to 3000 µN. Findings: Ultimate tensile strength of 1165 ± 20 MPa with ~18% elongation; ultimate compressive strength of 1863 ± 12 MPa with ~34% fracture strain.; B2 phase showed higher hardness (7.5 ± 2.2 GPa at 500 µN) compared to L12 phase (6.0 ± 0.5 GPa).; B2 phase exhibited higher strain rate sensitivity (SRS) than L12, with bulk SRS close to B2 values.; Micro-pillar yield strength was ~610 MPa for B2 and ~460 MPa for L12; mixed pillars showed double yielding at ~350 MPa and ~620-640 MPa.; B2 phase deformed via plastic barreling with limited slip steps, while L12 phase showed high density of slip steps and homogeneous flow.; Coefficient of friction was ~0.89 for B2 and ~0.83 for L12; L12 showed more material pile-up during scratch tests.; Phase boundary remained preserved without separation or cracking even after high compressive strains in mixed micro-pillars.. Mechanism: The B2 phase controls deformation due to its higher strength and SRS, while the L12 phase accommodates plasticity through multiple slip systems. The semi-coherent phase boundary prevents crack propagation and separation, contributing to high strength and ductility. Cr-rich nano-precipitates (~20 nm) in the B2 phase act as barriers to dislocation movement, enhancing strength. The tension-compression asymmetry arises from lamellar orientation, elastic property differences, and volume fractions of the phases.. Limitations: The study notes that multiple yield points were not detected in bulk tests likely due to the small difference in modulus between phases and lower resolution of bulk experiments. The anisotropic behavior may depend on the location of samples due to varying cooling conditions in the ingot.. Future work: The authors state these results will pave the way for fundamental understanding of phase-specific contributions to bulk mechanical response and help in designing structural materials with high fracture toughness.. Quote: "Dual mode fracture was observed with ductile failure for L12 phase and brittle mode for B2 phase."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the strength and deformation mechanisms of nanocrystalline Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy thin films (HEATFs) compared to bulk samples?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy thin films. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition on silicon wafer substrates; target cleaned by argon ion bombardment for ~2 min; substrate rotation speed 2 rpm; film thickness ~4 μm; nanopillars (diameter 738 nm) fabricated by FIB at 30 kV/10 pA. Test conditions: Room temperature; nanoindentation with Berkovich tip (depth <10% of film thickness); in situ SEM compression using flat punch diamond tip at strain rate ~5×10-3 s-1. Findings: Surface roughness Ra is less than 5 nm (specifically <3.5 nm in some profiles).; Grain size is approximately 10 nm with a homogeneous chemical composition.; Main phase is face-centered cubic (FCC) with a minor ordered BCC NiAl type phase.; Hardness is approximately 11.09 GPa, which is about three times that of bulk samples.; Elastic modulus is approximately 186.01 GPa, nearly the same as bulk samples.; Yield strength of nanopillars is approximately 1024 MPa, about three times that of bulk samples.; Compressive strength reached ~2075 MPa at a strain of ~11.39% before softening.; Plastic deformation is inhomogeneous and localized, occurring first at the top of the pillar.. Mechanism: The enhanced hardness is ascribed to the nanocrystalline strengthening mechanism induced by a large number of grain boundaries. The inhomogeneous plastic deformation is characterized by localized metal flow and slip generation at the top of the nanopillar.. Limitations: The text notes that a rigorous diffraction-intensity-distribution calculation of the solid solution phases responsible for certain orientations is beyond the scope of this work.. Future work: The results could provide an in-depth understanding of the mechanics and deformation mechanism for future design of nanocrystalline HEATFs with desired properties.. Quote: "The hardness and the yield strength of the high-entropy alloy thin film was about three times that of the bulk samples"

W2612952973.title: IOP Conf. Ser.: Mater. Sci. Eng. 117 012045

card: Paper card. Question: How can bulk soft magnetic materials achieve a combination of high strength and good ductility without significantly deteriorating their soft magnetic properties (specifically coercivity)?. System: Non-equiatomic Fe35-x/3Co30-x/3Ni30-x/3Ta5Alx (x = 3, 5, 7 at%) high-entropy alloys, specifically the 7Al-HEA variant with a face-centered cubic matrix and L12 nanoprecipitates.. Processing: As-cast plates (10-mm thick) were hot-rolled at 1473 K to 50% thickness reduction, followed by 10-min homogenization at 1473 K and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature; magnetic properties measured via vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) and magneto-optical Kerr microscopy; microstructure analyzed via TEM, APT, and 4D-STEM.. Findings: The 7Al-HEA achieved an ultimate tensile strength of 1526 MPa with a tensile elongation of 15.3%.; The yield strength of the 7Al-HEA (1202 MPa) was approximately 245% higher than the base alloy (501 MPa).; The coercivity of the 7Al-HEA was 10.7 Oe, only marginally increased from 8.6 Oe in the 3Al-HEA.; The saturation magnetization (Ms) of the 7Al-HEA was 88 Am2 kg-1, compared to 105 Am2 kg-1 for the 3Al-HEA.; The L12 nanoprecipitates had an average size of 13.5 ± 2.5 nm and a volume fraction greater than 42% in the 7Al-HEA.; Dynamic microband refinement reduced the mean distance between parallel microbands from 735 ± 251 nm to 163 ± 35 nm as local strain increased from 30% to 50%.; The 7Al-HEA maintained 61% of its room temperature Ms value at 773 K.; The lattice strain at the coherent interface varied between -0.2% and 0.5% for the 7Al-HEA.. Mechanism: Strength is enhanced by massive solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening via shearing of coherent ordered L12 nanoprecipitates, and dynamic microband refinement. Soft magnetic properties are preserved because the full coherency between the nanoprecipitates and the matrix creates negligible distortion fields, resulting in insignificant pinning of Bloch domain walls compared to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that conventional strengthening approaches usually significantly deteriorate soft magnetic properties due to Bloch wall interactions with defects.. Future work: The findings provide guidance for developing new high-performance materials with an excellent combination of mechanical and soft magnetic properties as needed for the electrification of transport and industry.. Quote: "Compared to the alloy in precipitate‐free state, the alloy variant with a large volume fraction (>42%) of nanoprecipitates achieves significantly enhanced strength (≈1526 MPa) at good ductility (≈15%), while the coercivity is only marginally increased (<10.7 Oe)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the limited ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) be overcome to achieve ultra-ductility while maintaining high strength?. System: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy consisting of FCC and B2 phases; industrial A357 casting aluminum alloy. Processing: Two cycles of 30% cold rolling followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 20 mins with water quenching; for A357: two cycles of 15% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins followed by two cycles of 30% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ tensile tests in FE-SEM; loading-unloading-reloading tests for back stress measurement. Findings: The phase-selectively recrystallized (PSR) EHEA achieves a uniform elongation of ∼33% and an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching ∼2.2 GPa.; The PSR EHEA exhibits a fracture true strain of ∼30%, which is double that of the As-cast (AC) alloy (∼14%) and the fully recrystallized (FR) alloy (∼17%).; The fracture true stress of the PSR EHEA reaches ∼1850 MPa, significantly higher than the AC (∼1390 MPa) and FR (∼1460 MPa) alloys.; The microcrack density in the fractured PSR specimen is only one-third of that in the FR specimen, even under a twofold nominal strain.; The local von Mises strain in the FCC phase can be up to 6 times higher than that in the B2 phase during deformation.; A back stress of ∼900 MPa near failure was quantitatively measured in the PSR EHEA, accounting for its high strain hardening capacity.; A B2 → body-centered tetragonal (BCT) phase transformation was observed in the PSR EHEA during deformation, with the crystal structure expanding ∼6% along the (200) direction.; The PSR strategy increased the elongation of the A357 aluminum alloy from ∼8% to ∼23% and doubled its tensile strength to ∼400 MPa.. Mechanism: Phase-selective recrystallization (PSR) eliminates weak boundaries (lamellar phase boundaries in AC and high-density grain boundaries in FR) by inducing complete recrystallization in the soft FCC phase while maintaining a skeletal, non-recrystallized B2 phase that undergoes only recovery. This microstructure prevents premature crack nucleation at weak interfaces, allowing both phases to contribute to strain hardening simultaneously through high-density dislocation multiplication and a strain-induced B2 to BCT phase transformation, thereby exhausting the alloy's strain hardening capacity before fracture.. Limitations: The proposed model for calculating the suitable deformation level for PSR is semi-quantitative because it ignores information on microstructure and strain rate.. Future work: Further modifications to the theoretical model to include microstructure and strain rate information; direct characterization of PSR behaviors under different rolling amounts and subsequent annealing to overcome the complexity of acquiring parameter values.. Quote: "The PSR EHEA with a well-tailored PSR microstructure doubles the fracture strain to ∼30%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can severe cryo-rolling followed by annealing be used to tailor heterogeneous microstructures and overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in brittle intermetallic-containing high entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNi2.1Nb0.2 high entropy alloy (FCC matrix with complex Laves phase particles). Processing: Homogenized ingots (1200 °C/24 h) were multi-pass cold- or cryo-rolled to 90% reduction in thickness (final thickness ~0.4 mm); cryo-rolling involved immersion in liquid N2 for 0.5 h before and after every pass; subsequent annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests conducted at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 using dog-bone shaped specimens.. Findings: Cryo-rolling resulted in a finer lamellar nanostructure with an average HAB spacing of ~50 ± 9 nm compared to ~65 ± 12 nm in cold-rolled samples.; The Laves phase particles showed greater fragmentation in cryo-rolled samples (average size ~0.68 ± 0.40 µm) compared to cold-rolled samples (~1.00 ± 0.44 µm).; The cryo-rolled and annealed HEA achieved a yield strength of 1219 ± 14 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1272 ± 25 MPa with ~22% elongation.; The cold-rolled and annealed HEA showed a yield strength of 774 ± 13 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1085 ± 18 MPa with ~20% elongation.; The yield strength of the cryo-rolled and annealed HEA was increased by ~400 MPa (~58% increase) compared to the cold-rolled and annealed HEA.; The cryo-rolled and annealed HEA exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure with co-existing deformed and recrystallized regions, whereas the cold-rolled HEA was predominantly recrystallized.; Profuse ε nano-precipitates formed early in the cryo-rolled HEA (after 120 s at 800 °C), inhibiting recrystallization via Zener pinning, while precipitation lagged recrystallization in the cold-rolled HEA.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous microstructure originates from accelerated precipitation of the nanosized ε phase early in the recrystallization process due to a greater density of nucleation sites (dislocations, shear bands, grain boundaries) in the cryo-rolled HEA; these precipitates pin high-angle boundaries (Zener pinning), inhibiting recrystallization and creating a mix of deformed and recrystallized regions; mechanical incompatibility between these domains generates strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs), creating long-range back stress that delays necking and enhances both strength and ductility.. Limitations: The back stress generated by the heterogeneous microstructure was not quantified in this study.. Future work: The authors suggest that the results indicate significant opportunities for achieving novel heterogeneous microstructures in a wide range of HEAs through innovative processing by cryo-rolling.. Quote: "Cryo-rolling resulted in a finer lamellar nanostructure and decidedly greater fragmentation of the Laves phase."

Question: Can a novel hybrid-rolling process combining cryo-rolling and warm-rolling create a dual structural-compositional heterogeneous microstructure in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy to achieve unprecedented strength-ductility synergy?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Hybrid-rolling consisting of two stages: Stage I cryo-rolling to a true strain of ~1.2 (90% reduction in thickness total) with samples immersed in liquid N2 for 30 minutes before and after each pass; Stage II warm-rolling at 600 °C to a true strain of ~1.2, with specimens held at 600 °C for 20 minutes prior to each of the ten passes and water quenched immediately after every pass.. Test conditions: Tensile tests performed along the rolling direction (RD) at ambient temperature using a universal testing machine with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1.. Findings: The hybrid-rolled EHEA achieved a yield strength (σYS) of ~1900 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (σUTS) of ~2000 MPa.; The hybrid-rolled EHEA maintained an elongation to failure (ef) of ~8%, which is more than twice that of the cryo-rolled material (~3%).; The specific strength of the hybrid-rolled EHEA was ~270 kNm.kg−1, at least 50% higher than commercial alloys like Ti-6Al-4V with similar elongation.; The microstructure consisted of retained lamellar regions (LRs) and adjacent nearly equiaxed nanocrystalline regions (NCRs) with an average grain size of ~240 nm.; The NCRs exhibited compositional heterogeneity with four distinct phases: L12 (NCR-1), disordered FCC (NCR-2), B2 (NCR-3), and Cr-rich B2 (NCR-4).; Approximately 70% of the grains in the NCRs were in a deformed state (KAM ≥ 1°), while ~30% were recrystallized.; The volume fractions of FCC and B2 phases in the as-cast condition were ~65% and 35%, respectively, with lamellae thicknesses of ~640 ± 40 nm and 240 ± 15 nm.. Mechanism: The extreme heterogeneities result from stored energy in cryo-rolled broken lamellar regions (BLRs) accelerating transformations during warm-rolling, creating dual structural (LRs vs NCRs) and compositional (different phases) heterogeneities. Mechanical incompatibility between domains with different hardness generates strain gradients accommodated by geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs), leading to long-range back stress that prevents early necking and enhances both strength and ductility.. Limitations: The authors state that the quantification of the back stress and its enhancement through further microstructural tuning remains a topic for future work.. Future work: The authors propose to evaluate the quantification of the back stress and its enhancement through further microstructural tuning in hybrid-processed dual structural-compositional heterogeneous EHEA.. Quote: "The novel processing strategy resulted in an extremely heterogeneous microstructure consisting of retained lamellar and transformed nanocrystalline regions."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the heterogeneous lattice strain field, caused by severe atomic lattice distortion in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), influence 3D dynamic dislocation evolution, strengthening mechanisms, and the strength-ductility synergy?. System: FeCoCrNiMn multi-principal element alloy (Cantor alloy). Processing: Arc-melting in high-purity argon atmosphere with raw materials ≥99.9 wt.% purity; remelted at least four times; cast into 10 mm diameter cylindrical ingots; heat treated at 1,200 °C for 30 h; micropillars milled via FIB with ~2 μm diameter, aspect ratio ~2, and taper angles <2.5°. Test conditions: Micropillar compression tests conducted at room temperature using a Hysitron TI 950 TriboIndenter; DDD simulations performed with ParaDiS code on a 5.5 μm cube with periodic boundary conditions at a strain rate of 10^4/s; lattice strain measured via Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA) on TEM images. Findings: Root-mean-square lattice strain shows a power law decaying relation with scan size, consistent with a fractal distribution of the residual strain field.; Heterogeneous lattice strain causes dislocation motion to become 'sluggish' with multiple pinning sites, raising dislocation density and entanglement probability.; Dislocations exhibit multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips (double cross slip) to minimize local lattice resistance.; The presence of heterogeneous lattice strain leads to a significant increase in yield strength compared to simulations without it.; Dislocation double cross slip results in the formation of dislocation walls and a unique multijogged dislocation configuration.; Yielding strengths predicted by DDD simulations for different crystallographic orientations are consistent with experimental micropillar measurements.; The root-mean-square lattice strain, extrapolated from high-resolution TEM images, correlates positively with the yield strengths of the MPEAs.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous lattice strain field creates a fluctuating elastic stress field that acts as pinning sites for dislocations. This forces dislocations to adopt wavy trajectories involving 'pinning-and-depinning' processes, which hinders smooth movement and promotes the formation of multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips. These behaviors increase dislocation density, entanglement, and forest strengthening, thereby enhancing strain hardening and enabling the strength-ductility synergy.. Limitations: The study does not account for the coupling of chemical short-range order (SRO) with lattice distortion, noting that while SRO may increase local shear strains, this is beyond the scope of the current work.. Future work: To address the effect of chemical short-range order (SRO) on local lattice strain and its coupling with lattice distortion in altering mechanical properties.. Quote: "Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the bulk critical resolved shear stress (CRSS), the size effect scaling exponent, the stacking fault energy, and the magnitude of solid-solution strengthening in the equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (FCC structure). Processing: Arc-melting of high-purity elements in argon, cold-rolling (60% reduction), recrystallization at 1,173–1,473 K; single-crystal micropillars (1.0–8.3 μm edge length) machined via FIB at 30 kV; bulk polycrystals with grain sizes of 8, 70, and 340 μm. Test conditions: Micropillar compression at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹); bulk polycrystal compression at room temperature and 77 K (strain rate 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹); TEM analysis at 200 kV. Findings: Bulk room temperature CRSS is estimated at 33–43 MPa, approximately 10 times higher than that of pure nickel (~3.2 MPa).; CRSS follows an inverse power-law scaling with pillar size with an exponent of –0.63, independent of crystal orientation.; Stacking fault energy is determined to be 30 ± 5 mJ/m² based on Shockley partial separations of 3.5–4.5 nm (screw) and 5–8 nm (edge).; Yield stress at 77 K (260 MPa for 340 μm grain size) is slightly more than twice the yield stress at room temperature (127 MPa).; Dislocations are planar and smoothly curved with no preferred line orientation, indicating no significant anisotropy in edge and screw mobilities.; The shear-modulus-normalized CRSS of the HEA corresponds to a hypothetical binary alloy with 20–50 at.% solute concentration and ~4% atomic size misfit.; Young's and shear moduli are ~10% smaller than pure Ni, while the bulk modulus is 24% smaller than pure Ni.. Mechanism: The high CRSS is attributed to thermal solid-solution hardening driven by atomic size misfit (~4% between Cr and Co/Fe) rather than severe lattice distortion alone; the low stacking fault energy combined with a high shear modulus leads to wide partial separations that inhibit cross-slip, while the absence of orientation dependence suggests similar mobilities for edge and screw segments.. Limitations: The study notes that Goldschmidt radii may not provide accurate size misfit values, requiring ab initio calculations to estimate the true misfit of ~4.1%; the solid-solution hardening estimate is described as a rough order-of-magnitude calculation.. Future work: The authors state that full results of deformation experiments on bulk single crystals of the HEA will be published elsewhere and that additional studies are needed to improve understanding of factors like impurity contamination affecting CRSS.. Quote: "CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it possible to introduce short-range ordering (SRO) in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to simultaneously enhance both ultimate strength and ductility, and what microstructures and mechanisms are required?. System: Equiatomic CoCuFeNiPd high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Hybrid Monte Carlo (MC) and Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations: MC site-occupancy swaps at 300 K and 1200 K using the Metropolis criterion, interchanged with MD relaxations (100 MC swaps followed by up to 100 MD relaxations per iteration) to optimize SRO; DFT calculations performed to validate cohesive energies.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile deformation simulations at strain rates of 2 × 10^8 s^-1 and 2 × 10^7 s^-1, at temperatures of 300 K and 1200 K; initial sample size 8788 atoms with lattice constant 3.6 Å.. Findings: The potential energy per atom decreased from -4.090 eV/atom (0 iterations) to -4.113 eV/atom (4 × 10^6 iterations), indicating energetically favorable SRO formation.; At 300 K, the ultimate stress increased from 3.4 GPa (no SRO) to 4.9 GPa (strong SRO), and ultimate strain increased from 6.0% to 9.6%.; SRO development led to the formation of three cluster types: FCC-preferred (FCCP), BCC-preferred (BCCP), and indifferent (IND) clusters.; FCCP clusters are primarily composed of Co (29 at%) and Ni (48 at%), while BCCP clusters are enriched in Fe (31 at%) and Pd (44 at%).; FCCP clusters withstand approximately 2 GPa/atom higher stresses than BCCP and IND clusters during deformation.; BCCP clusters undergo large plastic strain, acting as soft fillers, while FCCP clusters suffer relatively little plastic strain.; Strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations occurred in localized regions prior to the ultimate stress, driven by local compositional stability.; The presence of BCC-type structures prior to deformation was 2.4% for the 2 M sample and 3.0% for the 4 M sample, compared to 0% in the no-SRO sample.. Mechanism: The SRO creates a pseudo-composite microstructure where indifferent (IND) clusters act as a matrix, FCC-preferred (FCCP) clusters serve as hard fillers to enhance strength, and BCC-preferred (BCCP) clusters act as soft fillers to increase ductility. Deformation involves strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations prior to the ultimate stress, which increases work hardening, followed by dislocation slip within the untransformed FCC phase.. Limitations: The strain rates employed (2 × 10^8 s^-1) are very large compared with typical experiments, so the stress-strain curves should be interpreted as indicative of trends rather than quantitative values.. Future work: The authors suggest combining the SRO-based approach with larger-scale approaches (e.g., grain size, precipitates) to further optimize HEA mechanical response and exploring the effect of annealing temperature and grain boundaries on SRO and mechanical properties.. Quote: "Our results show that this HEA is energetically favorable to undergo short-range ordering (SRO), and the SRO leads to a pseudo-composite microstructure, which surprisingly enhances both the ultimate strength and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: How can twinning be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys with negative or very small positive stacking fault energies, challenging existing phenomenological models?. System: Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 (30 ≤ x ≤ 45), CrMnFeCoNi, and CrCoNi. Test conditions: Temperature range from 100 K to 500 K; affine shear strains of 0.8% and 1.2%; paramagnetic state modeled by disordered local magnetic moment approximation. Findings: For Fe80−xMnxCo10 alloys, twinning is favored over stacking faults when Mn content x ≥ 33, despite the fcc lattice being thermodynamically unstable (negative ΔF).; The metastable twinning (MTW) phenomenon occurs in CrMnFeCoNi between approximately 300 K and 460 K, where twinning is activated despite negative ΔF.; All three studied alloys exhibit γusf ≈ γutf with small or negative intrinsic stacking fault energy (γisf), a shape distinct from conventional fcc alloys.; Increasing affine shear strain increases the difference (γ¯SF - γ¯TW), thereby favoring twin nucleation; for CrMnFeCoNi, strains ≳0.7% induce MTW at all temperatures below ~460 K.; The twinning fraction (fTW) in alloys exhibiting MTW can surpass the previously established upper limit of 50%; for Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10, fTW is calculated to be 53%.; Classical SFE-based models fail to predict twinning in these systems because they require positive SFE > 10–16 mJ m−2, whereas MTW occurs with SFE values between -16.5 and 2.3 mJ m−2.; The condition for MTW is defined by δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where δ is the deviation from the universal scaling law and σ* is the pseudo-interfacial energy (approx. 4–9 mJ m−2).. Mechanism: Twinning is driven by the specific shape of the generalized stacking fault energy (γ-surface) where γusf ≈ γutf and γisf is small or negative, combined with the effect of inherent affine shear strain prior to slip. This strain increases the effective energy barrier for stacking faults relative to twinning, allowing twinning to dominate even when the fcc phase is thermodynamically unstable (ΔF ≤ 0). The phenomenon is governed by the condition δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where the chemistry and strain conditions allow the system to cross deformation mode boundaries that traditional models predict should lead to martensitic transformation.. Limitations: The study notes that while MTW is predicted for CrCoNi with increasing affine shear strain, the specific temperature range for this behavior was not fully explored in the provided text compared to the other alloys, and the analysis relies on theoretical calculations of intrinsic material parameters.. Future work: The authors propose that the disclosed behavior calls for a critical revision of previously adopted design criteria regarding twinning-induced plasticity and suggests opportunities for optimizing the mechanical response in engineering materials by tailoring metastable twinning.. Quote: "We demonstrate that twinning can be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic alloys with a fraction that surpasses the previously established upper limit."
